title: Can you treat mental illness with psychedelics?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore whether psychedelics such as LSD, MDMA (ecstasy), psilocybin, ketamine and ibogaine can treat mental illness. They trace the history: early LSD psychiatry in the 1950s (Hollywood sessions with Dr. Mortimer Hartman, Cary Grant, Esther Williams, Time magazine coverage), Alexander Shulgin's MDMA work, the later outlawing of LSD and MDMA, and George Ricaurte's retracted monkey study that helped justify banning ecstasy. They then cover modern studies in Switzerland, UCLA and Johns Hopkins showing promise for PTSD, depression, cluster headaches, addiction, and end-of-life distress (Pamela Seucda case), plus the serotonin hypothesis, the Bill W. LSD anecdote, and a caution that these are not endorsements. The episode closes with a CoED fundraiser plug and listener mail about octopuses.

segments.title: Opening banter and disclaimer
segments.summary: Hosts joke about a 1950s French mass-poisoning incident, give an official disclaimer that they do not endorse illegal drugs, and frame the episode as a follow-up to the MK Ultra LSD episode.

segments.title: Early history of LSD, MDMA and Shulgin
segments.summary: Albert Hofmann's discovery of LSD, MDMA's creation in 1914 by a Merck chemist, the CIA's lack of interest, and Alexander Shulgin's publication on MDMA and its spread to psychiatrists and the Dallas underground.

segments.title: Hollywood psychiatric sessions in the 1950s
segments.summary: Dr. Mortimer Hartman and Arthur Chandler's Beverly Hills psychiatric practice gave LSD sessions. Aldous Huxley, Cary Grant, Charles Brackett, Sydney Lumet and Clare Boothe Luce are discussed as LSD users, along with favorable Time magazine coverage.

segments.title: Cary Grant press and Esther Williams story
segments.summary: Look and Good Housekeeping articles praised LSD. Esther Williams describes a session with Dr. Hartman in which she had a hallucination involving her dead brother.

segments.title: Outlawing LSD and MDMA; Timothy Leary
segments.summary: Sandoz stopped making LSD and it was outlawed. Timothy Leary's public advocacy is blamed for hurting research. The hosts discuss the public turn against hallucinogens.

segments.title: George Ricaurte's retracted MDMA study and the Rave Act
segments.summary: Amid the crack epidemic, George Ricaurte published a study claiming MDMA causes serotonin depletion and brain damage, which fed scheduling and the Rave Act. His monkey study used methamphetamine by mistake and was retracted in Science; the NIDA ecstasy fact sheet was pulled.

segments.title: Modern psychedelic research: PTSD, depression, cluster headaches
segments.summary: Swiss and US researchers report studies of LSD, psilocybin, ketamine and MDMA. A twelve-person PTSD study found ten no longer met diagnostic criteria. Ketamine shows early promise for depression, and studies cover cluster headaches and smoking cessation. Johns Hopkins gave psilocybin to stable volunteers. The hosts discuss serotonin and why these drugs are thought not to be addictive.

segments.title: Risks, happy pills, and the Pamela Seucda case
segments.summary: Hosts discuss that psychedelics can worsen illness in predisposed people (Brian Wilson, Syd Barrett), the question of prescribing a happy pill, and a UCLA psilocybin case of a dying colon cancer patient, Pamela Seucda, who found renewed joy before dying in 2006. Ibogaine for opioid and cocaine withdrawal is mentioned, along with Bill Wilson's LSD use and public sentiment about legal versus illegal drugs.

segments.title: CoED fundraiser plug
segments.summary: Hosts promote a CoED Fall Fiesta fundraiser in Alpharetta, Georgia and describe CoED's textbook program in Guatemala.

segments.title: Listener mail about octopuses
segments.summary: A San Francisco aquarist writes about octopus enrichment and octopus kisses, and a sign-off about the sperm tentacle naming. The hosts close with a request for listener family sayings.
